name: Alutiiq
packetScope: Community/museum work only. Five proposed substantive cards, with naming and Traditions explicitly merging into collections reviewed in parallel; two new standalone works. No Site/canonical changes, contact or delegation.

sources.title: Alutiiq — What Is in a Name?
sources.annotation: A substantive museum lesson explains preferred names and their histories through several paragraphs, rather than a directory. It reflects the museum’s Kodiak perspective and recognizes variation. Merge with the root’s reviewed language-lesson collection; do not count another unit.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read actual identity/history paragraphs, web lines 40–43, and language-name/preference paragraphs 50–53, plus reference metadata. No cited dissertation, dictionary, journal article or linked lesson reviewed by this packet.
sources.mergeInstruction: Merge naming into the same conservative collection as root-reviewed grammar overview/pluralization/noun-stem lessons.

sources.contentReviewScope: Read introduction and actual Afognak, Karluk, Kaguyak and Port Lions accounts, web lines 45–79, 146–178 and 214–219. Other village entries are not claimed as fully reviewed.

sources.title: Self Determination at its Best: 50 Years of Service to the Chugach Region
sources.annotation: A regional tribal consortium’s own commemorative publication includes named leaders’ reflections on representation and services. It explicitly distinguishes Sugpiaq and multicultural member tribes. This institutional retrospective is not an independent outcomes evaluation or a statement that all regional peoples are identical.
sources.contentReviewScope: Read cover and printed pages 3,9–10; also selected timeline/service passages on printed pages12–17,24. Visually checked printed pages3,9–10 (PDF pages5,11–12). No full28-page or QR-linked interview review.

sources.dateBasis: Anniversary of 1974 founding and publisher filename, not a separately verified first-publication date.
sources.authorsNote: Institutional publication with reflections attributed to Fran Norman, Chief John Kvasnikoff, Esther Ronne and others; no single book author identified.

sources.title: Neq’rkat — The Wild Foods Cookbook
sources.annotation: This 2013 community recipe compilation credits individual contributors and museum collections. Selected entries show varied household approaches to harvested foods. It is cultural foodways evidence, not a universal traditional menu, medical advice or verification of every recipe’s food safety.
sources.contentReviewScope: Downloaded actual 72-page PDF; read cover/imprint, contents, printed pages 1–2, 7, 17, 32, 41, 53 and acknowledgements 64. Visually checked imprint and frontispiece iv; selected recipes were read as text.
sources.dateBasis: Actual copyright/imprint page, PDF page 2. The 2024 URL directory is not the book’s publication year.
sources.authorsNote: Community recipe compilation; named recipe contributors credited individually. Alisha Drabek is credited for cover and book design, not asserted as sole author.

claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Naming lesson identity/preference paragraphs; People introduction web lines50–53 identifies Unangan/Aleut as another coastal people.
claimBlocks.text: The museum explains that Alutiiq and Sugpiaq reflect people’s choices as well as colonial and regional histories. Kodiak leaders deliberately selected Alutiiq for the museum during cultural revitalization, while some people elsewhere prefer Sugpiaq. These preferences should guide how individuals and communities are described. A shared language tradition does not require everyone to use one self-designation, and historical use of Aleut across regions does not make Alutiiq/Sugpiaq and Unangax̂ people interchangeable.

claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Afognak and Kaguyak village entries; web lines 76–79, 176–178
claimBlocks.text: The museum’s village histories distinguish physical relocation from the end of a community. Afognak families moved after the 1964 earthquake and tsunamis, but the account describes continued visiting, harvesting and tribal culture camps. Kaguyak residents also resettled elsewhere after the disaster, often where relatives lived; the museum records continuing use of their homeland and a tribal council. These are specific Kodiak histories, rather than one settlement pattern that can be assigned to every Alutiiq community.

The museum distinguishes tribal governments from Native corporations and nonprofit service organizations. Its Kodiak examples include governments such as the Native Village of Afognak and the Sun’aq Tribe, alongside regional and village corporations. Tribal self-government, corporate shareholder relationships and nonprofit services are different forms of participation. One person may be connected with several institutions, so a corporation’s name should not substitute for identifying the government or community concerned.

Chugachmiut’s anniversary publication describes a tribal consortium serving communities that include Nanwalek and Port Graham. It distinguishes Sugpiaq from multicultural member tribes and connects locally directed services with self-determination. Reflections from community leaders explain why village representation matters in decisions about health, social services and cultural work. This account broadens an introduction grounded in Kodiak, while keeping the consortium, its member governments and their different identities distinct.

The museum’s 2013 cookbook presents foodways through named contributors rather than one standardized menu. Selected recipes combine harvested fish, berries and plants with ingredients used in contemporary households. Mary Haakanson’s first-fish soup and Patricia Mullan Kozak’s berry dish, for example, retain personal choices and family memories. The compilation offers evidence of living, varied food practices in a Kodiak publication; it should not be treated as proof that every Alutiiq family prepares or eats the same foods.

countingNotes: Five cards are not five automatically additional source units: naming merges into root’s language-lesson collection, and Tribes and Corporations merges into the history agent’s Alutiiq Traditions collection.
Villages is one collection despite multiple selected entries. The 2013 cookbook and 2024 Chugachmiut booklet are separate authored publications, not Traditions chapters.
The People landing page and inspected Sun’aq page stay supporting and outside the count. No count depends on reading an index description alone.
Quantity does not establish initial adequacy, community endorsement or completion. Do not add fillers to reach twelve.
geographyAndIdentityNotes: Kodiak Museum village and cookbook evidence concerns Kodiak communities. It does not automatically represent the outer Kenai Peninsula, Prince William Sound or the Alaska Peninsula.

Chugachmiut’s regional booklet supplies an additional Sugpiaq community perspective, including Nanwalek and Port Graham. Its constituency also includes distinct multicultural governments; do not relabel Eyak people or all Chugach-region citizens as Sugpiaq.

Sugpiaq and Alutiiq overlap as self-designations with personal and regional preferences. Unangax̂ remains distinct. No new political entity is inferred from the cultural label Alutiiq/Sugpiaq Nation in museum navigation.

Institutional descriptions distinguish tribal governments, ANCSA corporations and tribal consortium/nonprofit services. The word corporation in an organization’s historical name does not alone classify it as an ANCSA shareholder corporation.

dateAndSourceCorrections: Tribes and Corporations is a page in Alutiiq Traditions. A September2025 file path is not an established original publication date; the explicit September2022 statistics remain dated.
The cookbook’s actual imprint is2013. Its January2024 upload directory is not its publication year. Its PDF has72pages including front matter; the contents run to acknowledgements at printed64.
The Chugachmiut file identifies a June25,2024 revision; no exact first-publication date or current roster is asserted.
The Sun’aq guide is not silently repaired or republished as current. Its template images/text and “Guest User”/yearless date are disclosed in the excluded-supporting note.
Alisha Drabek is credited for cookbook cover/book design, not asserted as its sole author. Individual recipe credits do not establish that every contributor has the same ancestry.
coverageGaps: Additional direct voices from the Alaska Peninsula and distinct Prince William Sound/Kenai governments would improve geographic balance; two regional institutions do not represent every Alutiiq/Sugpiaq community.
Current tribal constitutions, recognition lists, corporation eligibility and land title were not audited.
No present-day population, fluent-speaker, stock-abundance or harvest-permit claims are proposed from undated pages.
Community-directed public art could be expanded in a later pass; no uninspected artist gallery, embedded film or catalogue is counted here.
Restricted knowledge, archaeological coordinates, ceremonial narratives and private enrollment information are excluded.
